Where it began

Brett Lee was born in Wollongong on 8 November 1976 and grew up in Oak Flats and Mount Warrigal, the middle one of three brothers. Their first pitch was the street outside the house, with a tennis ball and the garage door keeping wicket. His older brother Shane went on to play for Australia too. As a boy Brett looked up to Allan Donald and Dennis Lillee, and Lillee later became his mentor.

He was playing first-grade cricket at 16, went through the Australian Cricket Academy and made his first-class debut for New South Wales in November 1997. Steve Waugh, his state team-mate and Australia's captain, pushed hard for his inclusion.

The player

His Test debut, against India in December 1999, was the stuff of dreams. He took a wicket with his fourth ball and finished the innings with five for 47, the first Australian fast bowler since Lillee to take five on debut.

In 76 Tests he took 310 wickets at 30.82, with ten five-wicket hauls and a best of five for 30 against the West Indies at the Gabba. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 2006 and won the Allan Border Medal in 2008. When he left Tests only Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath and Lillee had taken more wickets for Australia. He won the 2003 World Cup and two Champions Trophies, and took the first hat-trick in Twenty20 internationals.

What made him special

Speed, above all. He was regularly over 140 km/h, could bowl whole spells above 150, and was once timed at 161.1 km/h against New Zealand. As the years went on he added a wide range of slower balls and cutters, and he learned that taking a little pace off could buy a lot of accuracy.

He could bat, too. Five Test fifties and an average of 20.15 made him a handy man in the lower order. His 43 not out at Edgbaston in 2005 so nearly won one of the great Ashes Tests, and the picture of Andrew Flintoff stopping to console him afterwards became the image of that summer. A Test hundred never quite came, although he got as far as 64.

Away from the middle

Music was his other love. He played bass and acoustic guitar in Six & Out, a band of former New South Wales cricketers that includes his brother Shane. He also wrote a song and recorded it in India with the singer Asha Bhosle, and it reached number two in the charts. He acted in films, commentated for Channel Nine and Fox Sports, coached bowlers for Ireland and Sri Lanka, and set up Mewsic, a charity that opened music centres across India. His old school at Oak Flats named its cricket ground after him.

And finally

He has been known as Binga since his school days, after the electronics chain Bing Lee. He celebrated many a bowled batter with an imaginary chainsaw, which must have been a cheerful sight for everyone except the batter.
